title: Determinants, Trace, and Volume Forms

Two of the most important invariants of an operator $\varphi$ on a finite-dimensional vector space, its trace and its determinant, were defined through matrices (Definitions [5.3.11](/notes/math-55a/5-3-change-of-basis#definition-5-3-11) and [5.4.20](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#definition-5-4-20)), and their independence of the basis needed a computation. Tensor products and exterior powers produce both of them without choosing a basis. Throughout this section $V$ is finite-dimensional.

## <span class="num">9.11.1</span> Trace as Contraction

Under the isomorphism $\End(V) = \Hom(V, V) \cong V^* \otimes V$ of Proposition [9.8.10](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-10), the trace becomes a natural pairing.

:::definition{9.11.1} Contraction
The ***contraction*** is the linear functional $$c : V^* \otimes V \to k, \qquad c(\ell \otimes v) = \ell(v);$$ it exists by the universal property, since $(\ell, v) \mapsto \ell(v)$ is bilinear.
:::

:::proposition{9.11.2} Trace as contraction
Let $\varphi \in \End(V)$, and let $\eta_\varphi \in V^* \otimes V$ be the tensor corresponding to $\varphi$ under Proposition [9.8.10](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-10). Then $$\Tr(\varphi) = c(\eta_\varphi).$$ In particular, the trace of the rank-one map $v \mapsto \ell(v)\, w$ is $\ell(w)$.
:::

:::proof
Choose a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ of $V$, with dual basis $(e_i^*)$, and let $A = (a_{ij})$ be the matrix of $\varphi$, so $\varphi(e_j) = \sum_i a_{ij} e_i$. The tensor $e_j^* \otimes e_i$ corresponds to the map sending $e_j$ to $e_i$ and the other basis vectors to $0$, whose matrix has a single $1$, in row $i$ and column $j$. Hence $$\eta_\varphi = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\, e_j^* \otimes e_i, \qquad c(\eta_\varphi) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\, e_j^*(e_i) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}\, \delta_{ij} = \sum_i a_{ii} = \Tr(\varphi).$$ For the rank-one map, $\eta = \ell \otimes w$ and $c(\eta) = \ell(w)$.
:::

:::note
Since $c$ involves no basis, this gives a basis-free definition of the trace: it is the composite $\End(V) \cong V^* \otimes V \xrightarrow{c} k$. The formula $\Tr(A) = \sum_i a_{ii}$ is what the contraction looks like in coordinates, and the invariance of the trace under change of basis becomes automatic.
:::

## <span class="num">9.11.2</span> The Determinant via the Top Exterior Power

Let $\dim V = n \ge 1$. An operator $\varphi$ on $V$ induces an operator $\bigwedge^n \varphi$ on the one-dimensional space $\bigwedge^n V$ (Proposition [9.10.6](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-6) and Corollary [9.10.9](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#corollary-9-10-9)). Every linear map $L$ from a one-dimensional space to itself is multiplication by a scalar: if $\omega$ spans the space and $L(\omega) = c\,\omega$, then $L(x\omega) = c\,x\omega$. For $\bigwedge^n \varphi$, that scalar is the determinant.

:::theorem{9.11.3} The determinant via $\bigwedge^n V$
Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $n \ge 1$ and $\varphi \in \End(V)$. Then $\bigwedge^n \varphi$ is multiplication by $\det(\varphi)$: $$\varphi(v_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge \varphi(v_n) = \det(\varphi)\; v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n \qquad \text{for all } v_1, \ldots, v_n \in V,$$ where $\det(\varphi)$ is the determinant of the matrix of $\varphi$ in any basis (Definition [5.4.20](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#definition-5-4-20)). More generally, if $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is a basis of $V$ and $v_j = \sum_i a_{ij} e_i$ for $j = 1, \ldots, n$, then $$v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n = \det(A)\; e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n, \qquad A = (a_{ij}).$$
:::

:::proof
Fix the basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$. Since $e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$ is a basis of $\bigwedge^n V$, each $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n$ is a unique multiple $D\cdot e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$, and we regard $D$ as a function of the $n \times n$ matrix $A$ whose $j$th column is the coordinate vector of $v_j$. It is multilinear in the columns, because the wedge product is multilinear and taking the coefficient of $e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$ is linear; it is alternating in the columns, because a wedge product with two equal factors vanishes; and $D(I) = 1$, since then $v_j = e_j$. By Theorem [5.4.4](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#theorem-5-4-4)(b), $D(A) = D(I)\det(A) = \det(A)$. This proves the second statement.

Applying it to $v_j = \varphi(e_j)$, whose coordinate vectors are the columns of the matrix $A$ of $\varphi$, gives $\bigwedge^n \varphi\,(e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n) = \det(A)\, e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$. As $e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$ spans $\bigwedge^n V$, $\bigwedge^n \varphi$ is multiplication by $\det(A)$, which is $\det(\varphi)$.
:::

:::note
The Leibniz formula can also be read off directly. With $v_j = \sum_i a_{ij} e_i$, multilinearity gives $$v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n = \sum_{i_1, \ldots, i_n} a_{i_1 1} a_{i_2 2} \cdots a_{i_n n}\; e_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{i_n}.$$ A term with a repeated index vanishes. The others have $(i_1, \ldots, i_n) = (\sigma(1), \ldots, \sigma(n))$ for a permutation $\sigma \in S_n$, and $e_{\sigma(1)} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{\sigma(n)} = \sgn(\sigma)\, e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$ by Lemma [9.10.2](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#lemma-9-10-2)(ii). Hence $$\det(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma)\, a_{\sigma(1)1}\, a_{\sigma(2)2} \cdots a_{\sigma(n)n},$$ which is the Leibniz formula of Definition [5.4.3](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#definition-5-4-3).
:::

:::note
We could have taken Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3) as the definition: $\det(\varphi)$ is the scalar by which $\varphi$ acts on the determinant line $\bigwedge^n V$. This definition needs no basis, no permutations and no cofactor expansions, so the independence of $\det(\varphi)$ from the basis is manifest. It also has a geometric meaning: $\bigwedge^n V$ is where signed volumes live, and $\det(\varphi)$ is the factor by which $\varphi$ scales them (see the end of this section).
:::

:::corollary{9.11.4} Properties of the determinant
Let $\dim V = n \ge 1$, $\varphi, \psi \in \End(V)$ and $\lambda \in k$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\det(\psi \circ \varphi) = \det(\psi) \det(\varphi)$.
2. $\det(\id_V) = 1$.
3. $\varphi$ is invertible if and only if $\det(\varphi) \neq 0$.
4. $\det(\lambda \varphi) = \lambda^n \det(\varphi)$.
:::

:::proof
(i) $\bigwedge^n(\psi \circ \varphi) = \bigwedge^n \psi \circ \bigwedge^n \varphi$ (Proposition [9.10.6](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-6)), and multiplication by $\det(\varphi)$ followed by multiplication by $\det(\psi)$ is multiplication by $\det(\psi)\det(\varphi)$.

(ii) $\bigwedge^n(\id_V)$ is the identity of $\bigwedge^n V$.

(iii) Let $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ be a basis of $V$. Then $\varphi$ is invertible if and only if $\varphi(e_1), \ldots, \varphi(e_n)$ is a basis of $V$, that is, if and only if these $n$ vectors are linearly independent; by Proposition [9.10.10](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-10), this happens if and only if $\varphi(e_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge \varphi(e_n) = \det(\varphi)\, e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$ is nonzero.

(iv) $(\lambda\varphi)(v_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge (\lambda\varphi)(v_n) = \lambda^n\, \varphi(v_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge \varphi(v_n)$ by multilinearity.
:::

Applied to the operators of $k^n$ given by two matrices $A$ and $B$, part (i) gives $\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)$, which is Theorem [5.4.7](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#theorem-5-4-7), now without any computation; part (iii) is Theorem [5.4.8](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#theorem-5-4-8). Neither argument is circular: the proof of Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3) used only the characterization of the determinant by its columns (Theorem [5.4.4](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#theorem-5-4-4)), which does not depend on multiplicativity.

## <span class="num">9.11.3</span> Exterior Powers of an Operator

The coefficients of a wedge product of fewer than $n$ vectors are determinants as well.

:::lemma{9.11.5} Coordinates of a wedge product
Let $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ be a basis of $V$, let $1 \le d \le n$, and let $w_1, \ldots, w_d \in V$ with $w_b = \sum_i a_{ib} e_i$, so that $A = (a_{ib})$ is an $n \times d$ matrix. For an increasing tuple $I = (i_1 < \cdots < i_d)$, let $A_I$ be the $d \times d$ matrix formed by the rows $i_1, \ldots, i_d$ of $A$. Then $$w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_d = \sum_I \det(A_I)\, e_I.$$
:::

:::proof
Let $p_I : V \to k^d$ send $\sum_i x_i e_i$ to $(x_{i_1}, \ldots, x_{i_d})$, and let $\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_d$ be the standard basis of $k^d$. The map $\bigwedge^d p_I$ sends $e_J$ to $p_I(e_{j_1}) \wedge \cdots \wedge p_I(e_{j_d})$, which is $\varepsilon_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_d$ if $J = I$ and $0$ otherwise (if $J \neq I$, some $j_b$ is not among the $i_a$, and $p_I(e_{j_b}) = 0$). So $\bigwedge^d p_I$ extracts the coefficient of $e_I$. On the other hand, the vectors $p_I(w_1), \ldots, p_I(w_d)$ are the columns of $A_I$, so by Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3) in $k^d$, $$\textstyle\bigwedge^d p_I\,(w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_d) = p_I(w_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge p_I(w_d) = \det(A_I)\; \varepsilon_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_d.$$
:::

Combined with Proposition [9.10.10](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-10), the lemma says that the columns of an $n \times d$ matrix are linearly independent if and only if some $d \times d$ minor of the matrix is nonzero.

:::proposition{9.11.6} Traces of exterior powers and the characteristic polynomial
Let $\dim V = n \ge 1$, and let $\varphi \in \End(V)$ have matrix $A$ in a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$. For an increasing $d$-tuple $I$, let $A_{II}$ be the $d \times d$ submatrix of $A$ with rows and columns $i_1, \ldots, i_d$; its determinant is a ***principal minor*** of $A$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\Tr(\bigwedge^d \varphi) = \sum_I \det(A_{II})$, the sum of the principal $d \times d$ minors of $A$.
2. The characteristic polynomial of $\varphi$ (Definition [7.4.7](/notes/math-55a/7-4-eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors#definition-7-4-7)) is $$\chi_\varphi(x) = \det(xI - A) = \sum_{d=0}^{n} (-1)^d\, \Tr\big(\textstyle\bigwedge^d \varphi\big)\, x^{n-d}.$$
3. If $A$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$, then $\Tr(\bigwedge^d \varphi) = \sum_{i_1 < \cdots < i_d} \lambda_{i_1} \cdots \lambda_{i_d}$, the $d$th elementary symmetric polynomial in $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$.
:::

:::proof
(i) The diagonal entry of the matrix of $\bigwedge^d \varphi$ in the basis $(e_I)$ at position $I$ is the coefficient of $e_I$ in $\bigwedge^d \varphi\,(e_I) = \varphi(e_{i_1}) \wedge \cdots \wedge \varphi(e_{i_d})$. The coordinate vectors of $\varphi(e_{i_1}), \ldots, \varphi(e_{i_d})$ are the columns $i_1, \ldots, i_d$ of $A$, and rows $i_1, \ldots, i_d$ of these columns form $A_{II}$; so the coefficient is $\det(A_{II})$ by Lemma [9.11.5](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#lemma-9-11-5). Summing over $I$ gives the trace.

(ii) The determinant $\det(xI - A)$ is given by the Leibniz formula, so it is the same polynomial whether we regard $xI - A$ as a matrix with entries in $k[x]$ or in the field $K = k(x)$ of rational functions (Example [5.4.25](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#example-5-4-25)). We work over $K$, in $K^n$ with standard basis $\varepsilon_1, \ldots, \varepsilon_n$. Let $a_j$ be the $j$th column of $A$; the $j$th column of $xI - A$ is $x\varepsilon_j - a_j$. By Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3) and multilinearity, $$\begin{aligned}
\det(xI - A)\; \varepsilon_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_n &= (x\varepsilon_1 - a_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge (x\varepsilon_n - a_n) \\
&= \sum_{S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, n\}} x^{|S|} (-1)^{n - |S|}\; w^S_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w^S_n,
\end{aligned}$$ where $w^S_j = \varepsilon_j$ for $j \in S$ and $w^S_j = a_j$ for $j \notin S$. Fix $S$, and let $I$ be the increasing tuple listing the complement of $S$, with $d = n - |S|$ entries. In $w^S_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w^S_n$ we may replace each $a_j$ ($j \in I$) by $a'_j = \sum_{i \in I} a_{ij} \varepsilon_i$, because the rest of $a_j$ is a combination of the $\varepsilon_s$ with $s \in S$, which already occur as factors. Let $\sigma \in S_n$ list the elements $s_1 < \cdots < s_{n-d}$ of $S$ followed by $i_1, \ldots, i_d$. Reordering the factors according to $\sigma$ multiplies both $w^S_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w^S_n$ and $\varepsilon_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_n$ by $\sgn(\sigma)$ (Lemma [9.10.2](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#lemma-9-10-2)(ii)). After reordering, the wedge product is $$\varepsilon_{s_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_{s_{n-d}} \wedge a'_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge a'_{i_d} = \det(A_{II})\; \varepsilon_{s_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_{s_{n-d}} \wedge \varepsilon_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_{i_d},$$ by Lemma [9.11.5](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#lemma-9-11-5): the coordinates of $a'_{i_1}, \ldots, a'_{i_d}$ vanish outside the rows in $I$, and in those rows they form $A_{II}$. Hence $w^S_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w^S_n = \det(A_{II})\, \varepsilon_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \varepsilon_n$, and $$\det(xI - A) = \sum_{d=0}^{n} (-1)^d\, x^{n-d} \sum_{|I| = d} \det(A_{II}) = \sum_{d=0}^{n} (-1)^d\, \Tr\big(\textstyle\bigwedge^d \varphi\big)\, x^{n-d}$$ by (i). (For $d = 0$ the inner sum is $1$, and $\bigwedge^0 \varphi = \id_k$ has trace $1$.)

(iii) Each $A_{II}$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\lambda_{i_1}, \ldots, \lambda_{i_d}$, so its determinant is their product (Proposition [5.4.10](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#proposition-5-4-10)); apply (i).
:::

When $k$ is algebraically closed, Theorem [7.5.2](/notes/math-55a/7-5-existence-of-eigenvectors-and-triangular-form#theorem-7-5-2) provides a basis in which $A$ is upper triangular; then $xI - A$ is upper triangular too, and $\chi_\varphi(x) = \det(xI - A) = \prod_i (x - \lambda_i)$, so the $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $\varphi$, each repeated according to its algebraic multiplicity, and (iii) says that $\Tr(\bigwedge^d \varphi)$ is the $d$th elementary symmetric polynomial in the eigenvalues. The cases $d = 1$ and $d = n$ are $\Tr(\varphi) = \sum_i \lambda_i$ and $\det(\varphi) = \prod_i \lambda_i$.

## <span class="num">9.11.4</span> Volume Forms and Orientation

Let $\dim V = n \ge 1$. Over $\RR$, think of the wedge product $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n$ as the signed volume of the parallelepiped $\{t_1 v_1 + \cdots + t_n v_n : 0 \le t_i \le 1\}$. It behaves as a signed volume should: it is multilinear and alternating, and it vanishes exactly when the parallelepiped is flat, that is, when the $v_i$ are dependent (Proposition [9.10.10](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-10)). But it lives in the line $\bigwedge^n V$, and turning it into a number requires an isomorphism $\bigwedge^n V \to k$.

:::definition{9.11.7} Volume form
Let $\dim V = n \ge 1$. A ***volume form*** on $V$ is a nonzero alternating $n$-linear form $\vol : V^n \to k$. By Proposition [9.10.5](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-5), volume forms correspond to the nonzero elements $L$ of $(\bigwedge^n V)^*$, that is, to the isomorphisms $L : \bigwedge^n V \to k$, via $\vol(v_1, \ldots, v_n) = L(v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n)$.
:::

Since $(\bigwedge^n V)^*$ is one-dimensional, any two volume forms differ by a nonzero scalar factor. A vector space has no preferred volume form until we give it more structure, such as an inner product.

:::proposition{9.11.8} Volume forms and determinants
Let $\vol$ be a volume form on $V$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\vol(v_1, \ldots, v_n) \neq 0$ if and only if $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ is a basis of $V$.
2. $\vol(\varphi(v_1), \ldots, \varphi(v_n)) = \det(\varphi)\, \vol(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ for every $\varphi \in \End(V)$.
3. If $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is a basis with $\vol(e_1, \ldots, e_n) = 1$, then $\vol(v_1, \ldots, v_n) = \det(A)$, where the $j$th column of $A$ is the coordinate vector of $v_j$ in this basis.
:::

:::proof
Write $\vol(v_1, \ldots, v_n) = L(v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n)$ with $L$ an isomorphism. (i) follows from Proposition [9.10.10](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-10), since $n$ independent vectors in $V$ form a basis. (ii) and (iii) follow by applying $L$ to the two formulas of Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3); in (iii), $L(e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n) = 1$.
:::

So $\det(\varphi)$ is the factor by which $\varphi$ multiplies all signed volumes, whichever volume form is used to measure them. Volume forms can also be written as wedge products of linear functionals.

:::proposition{9.11.9} Exterior powers of the dual space
For $1 \le d \le n$ there is an isomorphism $\bigwedge^d(V^*) \to (\bigwedge^d V)^*$ under which $\ell_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \ell_d$ corresponds to the functional $$v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_d \mapsto \det\big(\ell_i(v_j)\big)_{i,j=1}^{d}.$$ If $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ is a basis of $V$, it sends $e_I^* = e_{i_1}^* \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{i_d}^*$ to the dual basis of the basis $(e_I)$ of $\bigwedge^d V$. In particular, the alternating $d$-linear forms on $V$ are the elements of $\bigwedge^d(V^*)$.
:::

:::proof
For fixed $\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_d$, the function $(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \mapsto \det(\ell_i(v_j))$ is multilinear and alternating, because $v_j$ enters only the $j$th column of the matrix and the determinant is multilinear and alternating in the columns (Theorem [5.4.4](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#theorem-5-4-4)(a)); so it defines an element $f_\ell$ of $(\bigwedge^d V)^*$. For fixed $v_1, \ldots, v_d$, the value is multilinear and alternating in the $\ell_i$, because $\ell_i$ enters only the $i$th row and the determinant is also multilinear and alternating in the rows (Proposition [5.4.6](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#proposition-5-4-6)). Since $f_\ell$ is determined by its values on the spanning set of wedge products, $(\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_d) \mapsto f_\ell$ is multilinear and alternating, and it induces a linear map $\bigwedge^d(V^*) \to (\bigwedge^d V)^*$. For increasing tuples $I$ and $J$, the value of $f_{e_I^*}$ on $e_J$ is $\det(e_{i_a}^*(e_{j_b}))_{a,b}$. This is $\det(I_d) = 1$ when $I = J$; when $I \neq J$, some $i_a$ is not among the $j_b$, the $a$th row is zero, and the determinant is $0$. So the basis $(e_I^*)$ of $\bigwedge^d(V^*)$ is sent to the dual basis of $(e_I)$, and the map is an isomorphism. The last statement follows from Proposition [9.10.5](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-5).
:::

:::example{9.11.10} The volume form of a real inner product space
Let $V$ be a real inner product space (Definition [9.1.11](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#definition-9-1-11)) with an orthonormal basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$. The volume form $\vol = e_1^* \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n^*$ satisfies $\vol(e_1, \ldots, e_n) = \det(I) = 1$: the unit cube has volume $1$. By Proposition [9.11.8](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#proposition-9-11-8)(iii), $\vol(v_1, \ldots, v_n)$ is the determinant of the matrix of coordinates of the $v_j$.

Let $e'_1, \ldots, e'_n$ be another orthonormal basis, with $e'_j = \sum_i p_{ij} e_i$. Then $(P^t P)_{ij} = \sum_k p_{ki} p_{kj} = \langle e'_i, e'_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}$, so $P$ is orthogonal, and $\det(P)^2 = \det(P^t)\det(P) = 1$ by Proposition [5.4.6](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#proposition-5-4-6) and Theorem [5.4.7](/notes/math-55a/5-4-determinants#theorem-5-4-7). Hence $\vol(e'_1, \ldots, e'_n) = \det(P) = \pm 1$, and the volume form built from $(e'_i)$ is $\pm\vol$. So the inner product determines the volume form up to sign. Reordering an orthonormal basis can already change the sign: the basis $e_2, e_1, e_3, \ldots, e_n$ gives $-\vol$. Choosing the sign is choosing an orientation.
:::

:::definition{9.11.11} Orientation
Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $n \ge 1$. Two ordered bases $(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ and $(e'_1, \ldots, e'_n)$ of $V$ have the ***same orientation*** if $e'_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e'_n = c\; e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$ with $c > 0$. An ***orientation*** of $V$ is an equivalence class of ordered bases under this relation, and the bases in the chosen class are called ***positively oriented***.
:::

:::proposition{9.11.12} Orientations
Let $V$ be a real vector space of dimension $n \ge 1$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. Having the same orientation is an equivalence relation with exactly two classes. The constant $c$ of Definition [9.11.11](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#definition-9-11-11) is $\det(P)$, where $e'_j = \sum_i p_{ij} e_i$.
2. An orientation amounts to a choice of one of the two half-lines of $\bigwedge^n V \setminus \{0\}$, or of a volume form up to multiplication by a positive scalar.
3. An invertible $\varphi \in \End(V)$ sends positively oriented bases to positively oriented bases if and only if $\det(\varphi) > 0$.
:::

:::proof
(i) The formula $c = \det(P)$ is Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3). The relation is reflexive ($c = 1$), symmetric ($c$ becomes $1/c$) and transitive (the constants multiply), since inverses and products of positive numbers are positive. Fix a basis $(e_i)$. For every basis $(e'_i)$, the constant $c$ is nonzero (Proposition [9.10.10](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-10)), so it is positive or negative, and both signs occur, because replacing $e'_1$ by $-e'_1$ changes the sign of $c$. So there are exactly two classes.

(ii) The class of $(e'_i)$ is determined by the half-line of $\bigwedge^n V \setminus \{0\}$ containing $e'_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e'_n$. A volume form $\vol$ determines the class of the bases with $\vol(e'_1, \ldots, e'_n) > 0$, and $\vol$ and $c\,\vol$ determine the same class if and only if $c > 0$.

(iii) $\varphi(e'_1) \wedge \cdots \wedge \varphi(e'_n) = \det(\varphi)\, e'_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e'_n$.
:::

:::example{9.11.13} Orientations of the plane
In $\RR^2$, the bases $(e_1, e_2)$ and $(e_2, e_1)$ have opposite orientations, since $e_2 \wedge e_1 = -e_1 \wedge e_2$. Rotations have determinant $1$ and preserve orientation; reflections have determinant $-1$ and reverse it, which matches the description of $\mathrm{O}(2)$ in Proposition [9.5.16](/notes/math-55a/9-5-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators#proposition-9-5-16).
:::

:::exercise{9.11.14} Tensor products and multilinear algebra exercises
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Let $V$ be a two-dimensional vector space over $k$ with basis $e_1, e_2$.

   <!-- list:paren-alpha -->

   1. Write down a basis of $V \otimes V$, and find bases of the subspaces $\mcS^2(V)$ and $\mcA^2(V)$ of symmetric and alternating tensors when $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$. Verify that $\dim \mcS^2(V) + \dim \mcA^2(V) = \dim(V \otimes V)$, and find the alternating tensor corresponding to $e_1 \wedge e_2$ under Proposition [9.10.12](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-12).
   2. Suppose $\operatorname{char} k = 2$. Show that $\mcA^2(V) = \mcS^2(V)$ is three-dimensional, whereas $\dim \bigwedge^2 V = 1$.
2. Starting from the expression for $\det(A)$ obtained from wedge products in the note following Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3), prove that $\det(A^t) = \det(A)$ for every $n \times n$ matrix $A$.
3. Let $\dim V = n \ge 1$.

   <!-- list:paren-alpha -->

   1. Show that $\eta \mapsto (v \mapsto v \wedge \eta)$ is an isomorphism $\bigwedge^{n-1} V \to \Hom(V, \bigwedge^n V) \cong V^* \otimes \bigwedge^n V$; it involves no choices.
   2. Deduce that each nonzero $\omega \in \bigwedge^n V$ determines an isomorphism $\Phi_\omega : \bigwedge^{n-1} V \to V^*$, where $\Phi_\omega(\eta)(v) = c$ when $v \wedge \eta = c\,\omega$. How does $\Phi_\omega$ change when $\omega$ is replaced by $\lambda\omega$?
4. Let $V = \RR^3$ with the standard inner product and standard basis $e_1, e_2, e_3$, and let $\omega = e_1 \wedge e_2 \wedge e_3$. Compose $\Phi_\omega$ from (3) with the isomorphism $V^* \to V$ given by the inner product ($\ell \mapsto u$, where $\ell = \langle u, \cdot\, \rangle$). Show that the resulting isomorphism $\bigwedge^2 V \to V$ sends $v \wedge w$ to the cross product $v \times w$.

:::solution
**(1)** (a) A basis of $V \otimes V$ is $e_1 \otimes e_1,\ e_1 \otimes e_2,\ e_2 \otimes e_1,\ e_2 \otimes e_2$, so $\dim(V \otimes V) = 4$. The group $S_2$ has one nontrivial element, acting by the swap $\tau$. For $\eta = \sum_{i,j} c_{ij}\, e_i \otimes e_j$ we have $\tau\eta = \sum_{i,j} c_{ij}\, e_j \otimes e_i$, so $\eta$ is symmetric if and only if $c_{12} = c_{21}$. A basis of $\mcS^2(V)$ is $$e_1 \otimes e_1, \qquad e_2 \otimes e_2, \qquad e_1 \otimes e_2 + e_2 \otimes e_1,$$ and $\dim \mcS^2(V) = 3 = \binom{2+2-1}{2}$. The tensor $\eta$ is alternating if and only if $\tau\eta = -\eta$, that is, $c_{11} = -c_{11}$, $c_{22} = -c_{22}$ and $c_{21} = -c_{12}$. When $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$ this means $c_{11} = c_{22} = 0$ and $c_{21} = -c_{12}$, so $\mcA^2(V)$ has basis $e_1 \otimes e_2 - e_2 \otimes e_1$ and dimension $1 = \binom{2}{2}$. Indeed $3 + 1 = 4$, as Corollary [9.10.13](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#corollary-9-10-13) predicts. Under Proposition [9.10.12](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-12), $e_1 \wedge e_2$ corresponds to $P_\mcA(e_1 \otimes e_2) = \frac12(e_1 \otimes e_2 - e_2 \otimes e_1)$.

(b) In characteristic $2$ we have $-1 = 1$, so the condition $\tau\eta = -\eta$ is the condition $\tau\eta = \eta$: $\mcA^2(V) = \mcS^2(V)$, which is three-dimensional by the computation in (a) (that computation did not use the characteristic). But $\dim \bigwedge^2 V = \binom{2}{2} = 1$ by Proposition [9.10.8](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-8), which holds in every characteristic. So the subspace of alternating tensors is not a model of $\bigwedge^2 V$ in characteristic $2$. The subspace of symmetric tensors fails as a model of $\Sym^2 V$ as well, although its dimension is right: the quotient map sends $e_1 \otimes e_2 + e_2 \otimes e_1$ to $2\, e_1 e_2 = 0$, so it is not injective on $\mcS^2(V)$.

**(2)** By the note following Theorem [9.11.3](/notes/math-55a/9-11-determinants-trace-and-volume-forms#theorem-9-11-3), $$\det(A) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{j=1}^{n} a_{\sigma(j) j}.$$ The $(i, j)$ entry of $A^t$ is $a_{ji}$, so $$\det(A^t) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \sgn(\sigma) \prod_{j=1}^{n} a_{j \sigma(j)}.$$ For fixed $\sigma$, put $\tau = \sigma^{-1}$. As $j$ runs over $1, \ldots, n$, so does $i = \sigma(j)$, and $j = \tau(i)$; hence $\prod_j a_{j\sigma(j)} = \prod_i a_{\tau(i) i}$. Since $\sgn(\tau) = \sgn(\sigma)$ and $\sigma \mapsto \sigma^{-1}$ is a bijection of $S_n$, $$\det(A^t) = \sum_{\tau \in S_n} \sgn(\tau) \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_{\tau(i) i} = \det(A).$$

**(3)** (a) The product $(\eta, v) \mapsto v \wedge \eta$ from $\bigwedge^{n-1} V \times V$ to $\bigwedge^n V$ is bilinear (Definition [9.10.17](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#definition-9-10-17)). So for each $\eta$ the map $\Psi(\eta) : v \mapsto v \wedge \eta$ is linear, and $\eta \mapsto \Psi(\eta)$ is a linear map $\Psi : \bigwedge^{n-1} V \to \Hom(V, \bigwedge^n V)$. No choices were made. To see that $\Psi$ is injective, choose a basis $e_1, \ldots, e_n$. The increasing $(n-1)$-tuples are the tuples $I_j = (1, \ldots, \widehat{j}, \ldots, n)$ that omit one index $j$. Write $\eta = \sum_j c_j\, e_{I_j}$. For $j' \neq j$, $e_j \wedge e_{I_{j'}} = 0$, because $j$ occurs in $I_{j'}$; and $e_j \wedge e_{I_j} = (-1)^{j-1} e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$, by moving $e_j$ past $j - 1$ factors. So $\Psi(\eta)(e_j) = (-1)^{j-1} c_j\, e_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge e_n$, and $\Psi(\eta) = 0$ forces every $c_j = 0$. Both spaces have dimension $n$ (Proposition [9.10.8](/notes/math-55a/9-10-symmetric-and-exterior-powers#proposition-9-10-8)), so $\Psi$ is an isomorphism. Finally $\Hom(V, \bigwedge^n V) \cong V^* \otimes \bigwedge^n V$ by Proposition [9.8.10](/notes/math-55a/9-8-tensor-products#proposition-9-8-10).

(b) A nonzero $\omega$ gives an isomorphism $\bigwedge^n V \to k$, $c\,\omega \mapsto c$, and hence $\Hom(V, \bigwedge^n V) \cong \Hom(V, k) = V^*$. Composing with (a) gives $\Phi_\omega$. Since $v \wedge \eta = c\,\omega = (c/\lambda)(\lambda\omega)$, we get $\Phi_{\lambda\omega} = \lambda^{-1} \Phi_\omega$. So the isomorphism $\bigwedge^{n-1} V \cong V^*$ depends on the choice of $\omega$; the isomorphism of (a) does not.

**(4)** Let $v = \sum_i v_i e_i$ and $w = \sum_i w_i e_i$. Using $e_i \wedge e_i = 0$ and $e_j \wedge e_i = -e_i \wedge e_j$, $$v \wedge w = (v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1)\, e_1 \wedge e_2 + (v_1 w_3 - v_3 w_1)\, e_1 \wedge e_3 + (v_2 w_3 - v_3 w_2)\, e_2 \wedge e_3.$$ For $u = \sum_i u_i e_i$ we have $u \wedge e_2 \wedge e_3 = u_1\, \omega$, so $\Phi_\omega(e_2 \wedge e_3) = e_1^*$, which corresponds to $e_1$ because $\langle e_1, u \rangle = u_1$. Similarly $u \wedge e_1 \wedge e_3 = u_2\, e_2 \wedge e_1 \wedge e_3 = -u_2\, \omega$, so $e_1 \wedge e_3 \mapsto -e_2$; and $u \wedge e_1 \wedge e_2 = u_3\, e_3 \wedge e_1 \wedge e_2 = u_3\, \omega$ (moving $e_3$ past two factors), so $e_1 \wedge e_2 \mapsto e_3$. Therefore $$v \wedge w \mapsto (v_2 w_3 - v_3 w_2)\, e_1 - (v_1 w_3 - v_3 w_1)\, e_2 + (v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1)\, e_3 = v \times w.$$ The construction needs $\dim \bigwedge^2 V = \dim V$, that is, $\binom{n}{2} = n$, which for $n \ge 1$ holds only when $n = 3$. This is why it produces a cross product only in dimension $3$. (A bilinear cross product also exists on $\RR^7$, but it comes from a different construction.)
:::
:::
